messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 70
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Salesperson
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 35

He is 70 years old, married, and has spent most of his adult life working in sales, a role that has suited him because he is polished, attentive, and used to reading people quickly. He has built a long career on being calm, persuasive, and adaptable, qualities that now feel harder to access since he was assaulted. He tells the story in a steady voice, but as he talks, it becomes clear that the event still sits close to the surface for him, interrupting ordinary moments in ways that surprise him.

The assault happens abruptly, without warning, in the course of an ordinary day. He is moving through a public space when another man confronts him, and within seconds the situation turns physical. He remembers the shock first: the disbelief that this is happening to him, at his age, while simply going about his day. He is struck, shoved, and left feeling powerless in a way he had not felt since childhood. What stays with him most is not only the pain, but the humiliation. He describes the sense that his body fails him in the moment, that he cannot defend himself, cannot make sense of the violence, cannot even fully react before it is over.

In the days after, he tries to return to normal quickly. He has always been the type to keep moving, to show up, to handle things. He goes back to work and keeps his appointments, but he notices he is no longer as easy in his own skin. Driving now takes more concentration because he scans intersections and parking lots more than he used to. He sits with his back to walls when possible. When someone comes up behind him unexpectedly, his whole body jerks before he can stop it. He is embarrassed by how often he startles, and he tries to hide it, especially from his wife.

His work as a salesperson becomes more effortful. He is still able to talk with clients, but he finds himself distracted during conversations, missing details he would usually catch immediately. He used to enjoy the rhythm of meeting new people, reading the room, making a connection. Now there are moments when a sharp tone of voice or a sudden movement in a customer’s face sends a wave of tension through him. He keeps smiling, keeps the conversation going, but inside he is bracing, measuring the distance to the door, deciding unconsciously where he could move if needed. He notices that he is more tired after a day of sales calls because so much of his attention is spent monitoring for danger.

At night, the event returns in fragments. He does not always have a full nightmare, but he wakes with the feeling that something bad has just happened. Sometimes he sees the man’s face in a flash as he is falling asleep. Other times it is the sensation of being trapped, of not having enough room to move. He lies awake replaying the assault, wondering whether he should have done something differently, whether he looked weak, whether he made himself an easier target. He knows these thoughts are unfair, but they arrive anyway, and he cannot always push them away.

He has become more irritable than he likes to admit. Small frustrations land harder now. A delayed phone call, a driver cutting him off, a loud comment in a restaurant can leave him tense for the rest of the evening. His wife notices that he is quieter, more easily annoyed, and less inclined to join social plans. He still goes out with her, but he prefers places where he can see the entrances and exits. Crowds feel harder to tolerate. He has started avoiding certain errands if they require him to be in unfamiliar areas, and he makes excuses without fully explaining why.

Despite this, he keeps functioning. He gets up, dresses well, and returns calls. He still takes pride in being competent. But there is a narrowing in his life, a sense that he is organizing his days around not being caught off guard again. He does not describe himself as afraid in a dramatic way; instead, he speaks of being “on edge,” “not as relaxed,” and “always looking around.” There is sadness in that description, because he can see how much energy it takes to maintain the appearance of normalcy. What he misses most is the ease he used to feel moving through the world, the simple confidence of a man who assumed that if he stayed polite and alert, he would be fine.
